item.title: Investment Strategy Diversification
item.description:
By all conventional and even some unconventional measures, the US stock market is trading way beyond historical valuation averages and is closer to all time highs. Passive stock index investors have enjoyed a period of extraordinary gains in one of the longest running bull markets. No other major asset class has come close in the last 7 years. Well diversified portfolios have had lackluster returns while the stock market keeps making new highs.

Table 1: Performance by Asset Class
US Stocks Foreign Stocks US Bonds Foreign Bonds Treasuries Gold Commodities REITs
7 Years
  May 2010 - Apr 2017 Annualized Return 12.72% 4.47% 3.36% 0.79% 7.28% 0.66% -6.91% 11.09%
5 Years
  May 2012 - Apr 2017 Annualized Return 13.54% 5.40% 2.23% -0.61% 3.53% -5.69% -12.23% 9.16%
3 Years
  May 2014 - Apr 2017 Annualized Return 10.35% 1.09% 2.64% -3.14% 5.95% -0.93% -17.55% 8.82%

But overstretched valuations in a contentious political climate raise fears of what’s around the corner. Small market gains accumulated gradually over months could be wiped out within days or weeks, when the sentiment turns. So what should investors do?

Momentum strategies provide an attractive alternative in this scenario. Momentum has been described as a premier market anomaly. Studies have been published for over 2 decades showing why and how well it works. Despite being well publicized in the investment world, momentum strategies have continued to work well over long periods of time.

Some of the biggest advantages of momentum strategies are:

  • Their entry and exit rules could be well-defined and understood
  • They could be implemented using highly liquid, low cost ETFs
  • They are relatively easier to scale and execute
  • During market downturns, these strategies exhibit lower volatilities and drawdowns as compared to value and passive investing strategies

That being said, momentum is not a single monolithic strategy as many academics portray it to be. It could be implemented in many different ways. Here I present three momentum strategies that could be combined in simple ways to mitigate overall volatility and drawdowns, while maintaining attractive returns.

Global Equities Momentum Strategy

The first of these is Global Equities Momentum (“GEM”), which has been detailed by Gary Antonacci in his fantastic book, Dual Momentum Investing. It is one of the simplest strategies to understand and implement. GEM effectively makes use of zero correlation betweeen stocks and bonds. It utilizes absolute momentum to switch to bonds when stocks show weak performance, and bonds tend to do well. Additionally, it uses relative momentum to switch between domestic and foreign stocks during times of stock market strength.

Here are the concrete rules, dataset and assumptions to backtest GEM:

Rules : Between domestic and foreign equities, invest in the one which had higher outperformance relative to the risk free rate in the past 12 months. Otherwise invest in bonds.

Dataset : Total returns calculated from daily adjusted closing prices downloaded from Yahoo! Finance

  • Domestic stocks (SPY, combined with VFINX prior to Feb 1993)
  • Foreign stocks (CWI, combined with VGTSX prior to Jan 2007)
  • Bonds (AGG, combined with VBMFX prior to Oct 2003)
  • Risk free rate determined by T-bills data downloaded from FRED.

Assumptions : Signals and weights determined at the end of month (t), rebalanced at the end of first business day of next month (t+1), transaction costs 20 bps per trade.

Table 2: Comparison of GEM strategy with an equally weighted portfolio of SPY, CWI and AGG
SP500TR GEM_Antonacci GEM EqualWts
May 1997 - Apr 2017 Annualized Return 7.52% 12.66% 11.79% 6.24%
May 1997 - Apr 2017 Annualized Std Dev 15.17% 11.93% 11.97% 10.68%
May 1997 - Apr 2017 Annualized Sharpe (Rf=2.04%) 0.35 0.87 0.80 0.38
May 1997 - Apr 2017 Worst Drawdown -50.95% -17.84% -19.32% -38.77%

It is easy to cross-check the backtesting results with simulated results from Gary’s website. I do not expect to match the annualized returns as Gary’s simulations use theoretical indexes, do not apply any fees or transaction costs, and monthly performance numbers on his website are rounded to the first decimal place. But a correlation of monthly returns of 0.99, annualized standard deviations, shape of the equity curves and the close alignment of drawdowns all suggest a close match.

The GEM strategy performance shows simple rules could be used for timing entries and exits and work exceedingly well over complete market cycles. GEM trounces the S&P 500 Total Returns Index on both absolute and risk adjusted basis over 2 market cycles in this backtesting period.

The results of an equally weighted long only strategy of SPY, CWI and AGG are also shown. Essentially it’s a simplified and slightly aggressive 66.67% stocks and 33.33% bonds portfolio, which gives a sense of the performance of a passive structurally allocated portfolio strategy. As compared to the broader market, it does reduce the volatility but a worst drawdown of ~ 40% is still driven by stocks.

The edge provided by simple market timing rules in GEM is evident as compared to an equally weighted long only portfolio of the 3 underlying assets. The drawdowns are much lower as there’s a clear rule for exiting the market when it underperforms relative to the risk free rate. Moreover, there have been very few trades over the past 20 years, and most of the gains have been long term in nature. Hence GEM is quite attractive from a tax standpoint too.

SPY-TLT Universal Investment Strategy

This strategy has been detailed on LogicalInvest. It utilizes just 2 asset classes, stocks and long term treasuries, and takes advantage of a slighly inverse correlation between the two. While GEM rotates between stocks and bonds in a 100% risk-on / risk-off manner, this strategy is more nuanced. It rotates between stocks and long term treasuries in a more measured way. It selects between a mix of stocks and treasuries which has performed the best on a risk-adjusted basis, in the recent past.

Here are the concrete rules, dataset and assumptions to backtest UIS:

Rules : Construct 11 portfolios ranging from 100% SPY, 0% TLT to 0% SPY, 100% TLT, by successively incrementing the weight of TLT by 10%. Determine the returns and volatility of these 11 portfolios in the past 60 days (~ 3 months). Select the portfolio that gives the best risk adjusted returns in this period and apply the same weights to the following month.

Dataset : Total returns calculated from daily adjusted closing prices downloaded from Yahoo! Finance

  • Stocks (SPY, combined with VFINX prior to Feb 1993)
  • Long-term Treasuries (TLT, combined with VUSTX prior to Aug 2002).

Assumptions : Weights determined at the end of month (t), rebalanced at the end of first business day of next month (t+1), transaction costs 20 bps per trade.

Table 3: Comparison of UIS strategy with an equally weighted portfolio of SPY and TLT
SP500TR UIS EqualWts
Sep 1986 - Apr 2017 Annualized Return 10.01% 11.46% 9.12%
Sep 1986 - Apr 2017 Annualized Std Dev 14.99% 11.22% 8.83%
Sep 1986 - Apr 2017 Annualized Sharpe (Rf=3.23%) 0.44 0.71 0.64
Sep 1986 - Apr 2017 Worst Drawdown -50.95% -23.51% -22.35%

The performance of both UIS and an equally weighted long only mix of stocks and treasuries show the benefits of diversication between these 2 asset classes. In fact an equally weighted portfolio would’ve done just about as well as the S&P 500 Total Returns Index with far lower volatility and drawdowns. Since the global financial crisis of 2008, UIS has performed exceedingly well, which has led to its outperformance on both absolute as well as risk-adjusted basis.

Three-Way Momentum Strategy

This strategy is a more simplified version of a three-way momentum model posted by Meb Faber on his blog, that was originally done by Ned Davis Research. As Meb has suggested, it is conceptually similar to the strategies in his QTAA paper. This strategy is also one of the simplest to understand and implement. It utilizes just 3 asset classes: stocks, bonds and gold and invests equally in all asset classes that show positive momentum.

Here are the concrete rules, dataset and assumptions to backtest this strategy:

Rules : Invest equally in stocks, bonds and gold as long as they trade above their past 200 days moving average. If none of them trades above their 200 days moving average, then invest in T-bills.

Dataset : Total returns calculated from daily adjusted closing prices downloaded from Yahoo! Finance

  • Stocks (SPY, combined with VFINX prior to Feb 1993)
  • Bonds (AGG, combined with VBMFX prior to Oct 2003)
  • Gold (GLD, combined with LBMA/GOLD prior to Nov 2004).
  • Risk free rate determined by T-bills data downloaded from FRED.

Assumptions : Signals and weights determined at the end of month (t), rebalanced at the end of first business day of next month (t+1), transaction costs 20 bps per trade.

Table 4: Comparison of Three-Way Momentum Strategy with an equally weighted portfolio of SPY, AGG and GLD
SP500TR ThreeWay EqualWts
Nov 1987 - Apr 2017 Annualized Return 10.31% 8.60% 7.05%
Nov 1987 - Apr 2017 Annualized Std Dev 14.31% 7.57% 7.22%
Nov 1987 - Apr 2017 Annualized Sharpe (Rf=3.13%) 0.48 0.70 0.52
Nov 1987 - Apr 2017 Worst Drawdown -50.95% -13.34% -18.71%

Strategy Correlations

Although GEM works very well on its own, it is unlikely that the other two strategies could be followed on a stand-alone basis. Even the 100% risk-on / risk-off nature of GEM make it difficult to employ it at scale.

But let’s look at the correlations of these strategies:

Table 5: Correlation of monthly returns (May 1997 to April 2017)
SP500TR GEM UIS ThreeWay
SP500TR 1.00 0.67 0.26 0.35
GEM 0.67 1.00 0.31 0.55
UIS 0.26 0.31 1.00 0.37
ThreeWay 0.35 0.55 0.37 1.00

The UIS strategy has low correlations with both GEM and the Three-Way strategy. Even GEM and the Three-Way Strategy have a correlation of ~ 0.55. So they could be effectively blended together to form a portfolio of diversified strategies.

Here are a couple of simple ways to blend these strategies:

Strategy Blends

In the last 20 years backtesting period, an equal weight combination of GEM and UIS results in a significant reduction in portfolio volatility without compromising returns. Hence the blended strategy gets a solid boost on risk adjusted returns.

Table 6: Comparison of a blended strategy with 50% each of GEM & UIS strategies
SP500TR GEM UIS Equal_Blend
May 1997 - Apr 2017 Annualized Return 7.52% 11.79% 12.10% 12.20%
May 1997 - Apr 2017 Annualized Std Dev 15.17% 11.97% 11.15% 9.38%
May 1997 - Apr 2017 Annualized Sharpe (Rf=2.04%) 0.35 0.80 0.88 1.06
May 1997 - Apr 2017 Worst Drawdown -50.95% -19.32% -17.81% -11.81%

Combining GEM, UIS and Three-Way strategies on an equal weight basis, leads to even further reduction in portfolio volatility. At 8% it is closer to the lowest volatility of the three strategies. Even though the annualized return of the blended strategy is slightly lower than that of GEM, the risk adjusted return is ~ 40% higher.

Table 7: Comparison of a blended strategy with 33.33% each of GEM, UIS & ThreeWay strategies
SP500TR GEM UIS ThreeWay Equal_Blend

10 Years

Here are the equity curves and the distribution of weights in the blended strategy:

Advantages

There are many advantages of this blended strategy:

  • Works well in both bull and bear markets with low volatility
  • Uses low cost, highly liquid ETFs
  • With just 5 ETFs, it is very easy to implement and execute
  • Low cost substitute ETFs and funds exist to employ it at scale
  • Highly competitive with more complex strategies

Leveraged Blends

Given that the blended strategy exhibits very low volatility, the returns could be boosted by using leverage. To get a good sense of leveraged returns, I benchmark the margin rate at the prevailing 1-month USD LIBOR rate + 2%. This is well above the rates offered by brokerages catering to professional investors.

At the same level of volatility, the blended strategy would have produced over twice the returns of S&P 500 Total Returns Index, with much lower drawdowns.

Further Ideas

  • Scaling: Create weekly tranches, check signals and rebalance weekly instead of monthly. This way only 25% of the portfolio is exposed to whipsaw risk. Also, the trade sizes are reduced at any given point. I wrote about these ideas in a prior post.

  • Risk Management: From the weights plot of the blended strategy, it is evident that during some periods, 100% of the portfolio risk is concentrated in SPY. A prudent risk management strategy would limit the concentration on any single asset in a portfolio. So sudden unfavorable movements have less of an impact.

  • Add more uncorrelated strategies: Instead of being all-in on momentum only, value strategies could be added to the mix, which exhibit low correlation to momentum strategies.

  • Alternative Implementation: Implement this strategy using futures products which provide greater control over margins to scale up or down.

Conclusion

Investors are either totally passive or too fixated on finding a single unicorn strategy that’ll work well during both good and bad times. The key is to put together a team of sufficiently uncorrelated strategies that work well together to build a robust portfolio.

item.title: Luck in Rebalance Timing
item.description:
An important and often overlooked topic was raised by Corey Hoffstein at NewFound Research. Here are his first couple of tweets on that topic:

Indeed, this is about rebalance timing and how little attention it gets. Within the construct of a systematic strategy, this is a part of the Execution Model.

The Black Box Revealed

Courtesy: Inside the Black Box - The Simple Truth about Quantitative Trading by Rishi Narang

Unless it’s an intraday trading model, when it comes to portfolio rebalancing, a common convention is to rebalance at the beginning of a new month. Perhaps, these are some of the reasons behind this convention:

  1. In published literature, a monthly period is commonly used for portfolio rebalancing. Hence it has become a sort of common convention to follow.
  2. Most of the researchers are adept in using Excel, but less so in programming languages. While doing a backtest in Excel, it is easier to manipulate monthly data and do performance analysis, as opposed doing it with daily data.
  3. In some cases, investible products for some asset classes have not existed beyond a couple of decades at best. So longer backtests are often done using theoretical indices which are often available only in monthly format. Hence it forces the choice of a monthly rebalancing cycle. This implies rebalancing at the beginning of a new month.

But should this be accepted just on the basis of a common convention? If a monthly rebalancing cycle is adopted, does it matter which day of the month is chosen for rebalance? Are there any major differences between portfolios rebalanced on the first business day of a month, as opposed to other days? Are these differences just completely random in nature?

These are some of the questions that need to be answered.

Strategy

To answer these questions, I used one of the most basic market timing strategies:

Go long S&P500 when it trades above its 200 days simple moving average (SMA), otherwise exit and invest in T-Bills.

There is nothing magical about using a 200 days SMA. Other periods in the same ballpark work just as well, as shown by Meb Faber in his QTAA paper. I used this simple strategy to illustrate the effect of rebalance timing on portfolio performance.

I put together a historical daily total returns dataset of SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY), spliced together with historical daily total returns data of Vanguard 500 Index fund (VFINX), prior to Feb. 1993. This data was sourced from Yahoo! Finance, prior to their API fiasco earlier this month. Both of these products closely track the S&P500 Total Returns Index. This provides 37+ years of historical daily total returns data going back to the beginning of 1980.

Methodology

To test the effect of rebalance timing, I constructed 21 portfolio series, assuming 21 business days in a month. The first portfolio series is rebalanced on the first business day of a month, using the trading signal as of the end of the previous month. In short, signal @ t, rebalance @ t+1. If there are fewer than 21 business days in a month, say for instance 19 days, then portfolio series 20 and 21 are rebalanced on the first business day of the next month. A transaction cost of 10 bps is applied on each trade.

Here are the results:

The impact of luck could be observed in drawdowns as well as returns. The worst drawdown of series 13 is just a little more than half of series 14. Nevertheless, their annualized returns are almost the same. In all the cases, except series 13, the worst drawdown happened after the crash of 1987. Ironically, series 13 is the lucky one here ;). As Corey mentioned in his tweets, for an investment manager this is a difference between getting hired and fired.

At the moment, series 1, gives the best return. As we progress to series 9, the returns decrease quite significantly. There is a difference of over 2% in their annualized returns. Here are their performance summaries:

Table 1: Best and worst rebalance series
Best Worst
ALL Years
  Jan 1981 - Apr 2017 Annualized Return 10.68% 8.63%
  Jan 1981 - Apr 2017 Annualized Std Dev 11.09% 11.87%
  Jan 1981 - Apr 2017 Annualized Sharpe (Rf=4.22%) 0.55 0.35
  Jan 1981 - Apr 2017 Worst Drawdown -23.59% -26.20%

Let’s take a look at how the best (blue) and the worst (red) series have fared relative to the other 19 series in the entire historical period:

So, turns out the current best performed worse than the median for most of the historical period. But since 2003, it really took off and has managed to avoid many whipsaws that appear to have affected other series. But will it continue to do better? The impact of luck is quite obvious here. Quite surprisingly, the worst series has been at or near the worst throughout the historical period. Perhaps a longer backtest or one with a different investment strategy would be useful to investigate this further.

Mitigating the impact of luck

So how could the impact of luck be mitigated without resorting to more frequent rebalancing, and thus incurring higher portfolio turnover costs?

Here are a couple of ideas:

  1. Create four weekly portfolio series staggered by a week, where each series is rebalanced at the interval of 4 weeks. This way, at any given time, only ~ 25% of the capital is exposed to whipsaw risk. But a practical challenge here is to ensure that each series remains balanced relative to others. Say for instance, no single series should have a weight greater than a third of the entire portfolio. This could be managed by leveraging / deleveraging at rebalance time.

  2. Stick with rebalancing at the beginning of a new month (t+1). But instead of taking the signal at the last day of the prior month (t), take the median (or mean) of the daily signals in the prior month. This is similar to Corey’s idea of signal smoothing with 21 days SMA of signals.

Let’s see how these methods compare to the best and worst portfolios:

The three methods with overlapping portfolios and signal smoothing are denoted by Weekly_avg, Signal_median, Signal_avg. We can observe that all of these methods have similar performance profiles in the historical period, with minor differences in shorter time periods. They perform much better than the Worst portfolio series, in all time periods. And during most of the historical period, they have even performed better than the current Best series.

As we can see, relatively simple solutions work well to mitigate the impact of luck in rebalance timing.

item.title: Building a Predictive Typing Model
item.description:
Everyone using a smartphone or a mobile device has used an onscreen smart keyboard that tries to predict the next set of words that the user might want to type. Typically, upto 3 words are predicted, which are displayed in a row at the top of the keyboard. Given that typing on a glass pane without tactile feedback, could be very frustrating at times, the smart keyboard goes a long way in alleviating these issues.

But, how does predictive typing work? Basically, it’s a predictive typing model built using an ngram with backoff prediction model. Makes complete sense, right? Well, it’s less complicated than it sounds, and actually not hard to understand, as we shall see further.

Corpus

To begin, we need a large corpus of text with a wide-ranging vocabulary. The first name that comes to mind is that of William Shakespeare. Shakespeare wrote a number of plays and poems that are classics in the English language. These plays and poems are available in the public domain and are easily accessible through a number of sources, (see here and here). By some accounts, Shakespeare’s vocabulary ranged from 15,000-30,000 words, which makes it excellent to use it for our corpus.

David Robinson’s gutenbergr package makes it easy to download ‘The Complete Works Of Shakespeare’, from Project Gutenberg’s website. The downloaded dataset is a data frame with text appearing in rows along with the gutenberg id.

dfRaw <- gutenberg_download(100)
knitr::kable(head(dfRaw, 12))
gutenberg_id text
100 Shakespeare
100
100 This Etext has certain copyright implications you should read!
100
100 <<THIS ELECTRONIC VERSION OF THE COMPLETE WORKS OF WILLIAM
100 SHAKESPEARE IS COPYRIGHT 1990-1993 BY WORLD LIBRARY, INC., AND IS
100 PROVIDED BY PROJECT GUTENBERG ETEXT OF ILLINOIS BENEDICTINE COLLEGE
100 WITH PERMISSION. ELECTRONIC AND MACHINE READABLE COPIES MAY BE
100 DISTRIBUTED SO LONG AS SUCH COPIES (1) ARE FOR YOUR OR OTHERS
100 PERSONAL USE ONLY, AND (2) ARE NOT DISTRIBUTED OR USED
100 COMMERCIALLY. PROHIBITED COMMERCIAL DISTRIBUTION INCLUDES BY ANY
100 SERVICE THAT CHARGES FOR DOWNLOAD TIME OR FOR MEMBERSHIP.>> 
knitr::kable(dfRaw[sample(nrow(dfRaw), 6),])
gutenberg_id text
100 Assure yourselves, will never be unkind.
100
100 Like one besotted on your sweet delights.
100 And spurn in pieces posts of adamant;
100 Whereto, when they shall know what men are rich,
100 TITUS. Marcus, even thou hast struck upon my crest,

Data Preparation

The copyright notice appears multiple times throughout the text. Fortunately, it doesn’t prevent us from using this data for non-commercial purposes. The first step is to merge the entire text and remove the copyright notices that are helpfully within << … >>. Secondly, in plays, the characters and their relationships and titles are defined with ‘DRAMATIS PERSONAE’. These lines have to be removed too.

After doing some quick cleaning, the text is reconverted to a data frame.

complete_works <- str_c(dfRaw$text, collapse = ".")
complete_works <- str_split(complete_works, "<<[^>]*>>")[[1]]
complete_works <- complete_works[!(str_detect(complete_works, "Dramatis Personae|DRAMATIS PERSONAE"))]
complete_works <- str_replace_all(complete_works, "\\[|\\]", ".")

dfContent <- as_tibble(complete_works) %>% slice(3:n())
rm(complete_works)

Finally, we parse the content into sentences. The tidytext package by David Robinson and Julia Silge, is most useful in doing this within the tidyverse framework.

Here’s what the function does below:

  • Replaces all ‘logical’ sentence break delimiters by a period for easier tokenization by sentence
  • Removes extra periods and spaces
  • Tokenizes into sentences
  • Removes all sentences containing ACT or SCENE
  • Removes all digits from sentences
  • Finally adds line numbers to each row (more on the importance of this later…)

A sample of 10 sentences is shown below.

getSentences <- function(dfContent) {
    df <- dfContent %>% 
        mutate(value = str_replace_all(value, ";|:|!|\\?| \\-|\\- | \\- ", "\\. ")) %>% 
        mutate(value = str_replace_all(value, "[\\.]+", "\\.")) %>% 
        mutate(value = str_replace_all(value, "[[:space:]]+", " ")) %>% 
        unnest_tokens(sentence, value, token = "sentences", to_lower = FALSE) %>% 
        dplyr::filter(!str_detect(sentence, "Act|ACT|Scene|SCENE")) %>% 
        mutate(sentence = str_replace_all(sentence, "[0-9]","")) %>% 
        mutate(lineNumber = row_number()) %>% 
        select(lineNumber, everything())
}

dfSentences <- getSentences(dfContent)
knitr::kable(dfSentences[sample(nrow(dfSentences), 10),])
lineNumber sentence
55991 That with the King here resteth in his tent. .
16097 You are a merry man, sir. fare you well.
9717 He did ask favour.
100749 To the health of our general. .
40908 You are, I think, assur’d I love you not.
117828 Laurence. and another Watchman.
19243 Ere now denied the asker, and now again,.
145024 I swear to do this, though a present death.
70942 Stocking his messenger.
122957 For bringing wood in slowly.

Creating ngrams

“ngrams are a contiguous sequence of n items from a given sequence of text…” - Wikipedia

In this case, ngrams would be a contiguous sequence of n words. In the simplest form, an ngram of size 1 is a single word. An ngram of size 2 or more is a set of words that appear one after the other in a sequence.

For instance, given a sentence - how are you doing?

  • There are 4 Unigrams: how, are, you, doing
  • There are 3 Bigrams: how are, are you, you doing
  • There are 2 Trigrams: how are you, are you doing
  • There is 1 Quadrigram: how are you doing

So, using the data frame of clean sentences that we parsed, the next step is to create ngrams. Once again this is made simple using the unnest_tokens function from the tidytext package. And this is where grouping by line numbers is important because we want ngrams to be created by sequence of words, only within the same line. We do not want ngrams connected by a sentence break.

getNgrams <- function(dfSentences, n) {
    dfNgrams <- dfSentences %>% 
        group_by(lineNumber) %>% 
        unnest_tokens(word, sentence, token = "ngrams", n = n) %>% 
        ungroup() %>% 
        count(word, sort = TRUE) %>% 
        rename(freq = n)
}

All Words

df1grams <- getNgrams(dfSentences, 1)
dim(df1grams)
[1] 26453     2
wordsOfFreq1 <- df1grams %>% group_by(freq) %>% summarise(n = sum(freq)) %>% dplyr::filter(freq == 1) %>% .$n

There are 26453 words in the corpus, that shows how vast Shakespeare’s vocabulary was. Let’s see a wordcloud of top 100 words. No surprise, the most commonly used words are: the, and, i, to, of. Excluding these commonly used ‘stop words’, in the second wordcloud, we can see the words Shakespeare used most frequently. We can see a lot of references to royalty and nobility, present specially in Shakespearean tragedies. Some names are mentioned quite frequently - Richard, John, Caesar, Brutus and Henry. Some English counties or shires are mentioned quite often - Warwick, York and Gloucester.

Unigrams

Let’s see a plot of the distribution of words in corpus by usage.

Here’s a strategy for building ngram tables:

  • There is a long tail of 10522 words in the corpus that appear exactly once. Replace all words appearing just once, by UNK as a placeholder for a word not known from the corpus. There are a couple of motivations behind this:
    • It reduces the size of ngram tables.
    • More importantly, when an unknown word is encountered, the model knows how to tackle it before predicting the next set of words.
  • Re-summarise and rearrange the table by frequency.
  • Assign an index to each word.
  • Convert to data.table format. Some of the biggest benefits of this approach are:
    • Rows could be assigned and referenced by a key. This makes it extremely simple to look up a row value.
    • Lookup by a key is very fast compared to matching character strings.
    • When we create tables for bigrams and higher order ngrams, we can replace the words by their corresponding integer indexes. It saves a lot of memory as compared to creating tibbles with character strings.
vTopUnigrams <- df1grams %>% dplyr::filter(freq >= 2) %>% .$word
df1grams <- df1grams %>% 
    mutate(word = ifelse(word %in% vTopUnigrams, word, "UNK")) %>% 
    group_by(word) %>% 
    summarise(freq = sum(freq)) %>% 
    arrange(desc(freq)) %>% 
    mutate(index1 = row_number()) %>% 
    select(index1, freq, word)

dt1grams <- as.data.table(df1grams)
# set key to word
dt1grams <- dt1grams[,.(index1,freq),key=word]
# create another table with key=index1
dt1gramsByIndex <- dt1grams[,.(word,freq),key=index1]
# print dimensions
dim(dt1grams)
[1] 15932     3

Bigrams

A data table of bigrams is created where the index of the first word is the lookup key. The second word cannot be UNK since it is a word used for making predictions from the bigram table.

df2grams <- getNgrams(dfSentences, 2) %>% 
    separate(word, c("word1", "word2"), sep = " ") %>% 
    mutate(word1 = ifelse(word1 %in% vTopUnigrams, word1, "UNK")) %>% 
    dplyr::filter(word2 %in% vTopUnigrams) %>% 
    group_by(word1, word2) %>% 
    summarise(freq = sum(freq)) %>% 
    arrange(desc(freq))

dt2grams <- as.data.table(df2grams)
dt2grams$index1 <- dt1grams[dt2grams$word1]$index1
dt2grams$index2 <- dt1grams[dt2grams$word2]$index1
dt2grams <- dt2grams[,.(index1,index2,freq)]
setkey(dt2grams, index1)

Trigrams

Similarly, a data table of trigrams is created where indexes of the first and second words form the lookup key. The third word cannot be UNK since it is a word used for making predictions from the trigram table.

df3grams <- getNgrams(dfSentences, 3) %>% 
    separate(word, c("word1", "word2", "word3"), sep = " ") %>% 
    mutate(word1 = ifelse(word1 %in% vTopUnigrams, word1, "UNK")) %>%

    dplyr::filter(word3 %in% vTopUnigrams) %>%

dt3grams$index1 <- dt1grams[dt3grams$word1]$index1

dt3grams$index3 <- dt1grams[dt3grams$word3]$index1

setkey(dt3grams, index1,index2)

These ngram tables comprise all the information needed for the prediction model.

Memory Usage Comparison

As mentioned above, storing words as integer indexes in a data table is far more efficient as compared to a data frame with character strings. For instance, here’s how a pentagram data table looks like that contains just the integer indexes of the words:

index1 index2 index3 index4 index5 freq

print(object.size(df1grams)+object.size(df2grams)+object.size(df3grams)+
          object.size(df4grams)+object.size(df5grams), units = "auto")
158 Mb

print(object.size(dt1grams)+object.size(dt1gramsByIndex)+object.size(dt2grams)+object.size(dt3grams)+
          object.size(dt4grams)+object.size(dt5grams), units = "auto")
30.4 Mb

Ngram With Backoff Prediction Algorithm

So, given the ngram data tables, here’s how the prediction algorithm works:

  • Sanitize the input text as done above
  • Parse the text into sentences
  • Determine the words in the last sentence of the input text. Use upto the last 4 words from the input text.
  • The word predictions are done starting from the ngram table containing the longest sequence of words, provided the input text contains atleast n-1 words. So, if the last 4 words from the input text match the first 4 words in the pentagram table, then the fifth word is chosen, that has the highest frequency of occurance after those 4 words. If more than one word prediction is desired, then the fifth words with the next highest frequency of occurance are also chosen.
  • If no matches or fewer than desired number of matches are found in the pentagram table, then the algorithm backoffs to the quadrigram table using the last 3 words typed, then to the trigram table using the last 2 words typed, then to the bigram table using the last word typed and finally to the unigram table, until the desired number of word predictions are returned.

Let’s see how this works concretely with some test cases:

Test Cases

The first test is to confirm whether the word predictions from the unigram table, match with what we expect. The top 10 unigram table contains 3 words beginning with the letter ‘t’ - the(1), to(4), that(10). And sure enough, this is what we get from our prediction function.

[1] "Top 3 Final Predictions: not,a,sure"

Now let’s examine the UNK feature. We know that the UNK of is number 5 most common sequence in the trigram table so we should expect to see ‘of’ as the first prediction if the input text has an unknown word after ‘the’. So let’s input some gibberish after ‘the’ to make sure this word doesn’t exist in our vocabulary:

[1] "Top 3 Final Predictions: of,and,in"

Using one of the most well known speeches from Hamlet, we can see that the algorithm gets the first word prediction from the pentagram table. But since we are looking for the next 3 words, the algorithm backoffs to predictions from quadrigram and trigram tables, until it has atleast 3 words. In this case, the pentagram table gives us the best match that we are looking for. We can also observe that once we have atleast 4 words in our input text, the words prior to those do not matter for the next word predictions.

item.title: Ames Housing - Part 2 - Building Models
item.description:
In a previous post in this series, we explored the Ames Housing dataset.

In this post, we build linear and non-linear models, and we find out how well they predict the SalePrice of properties. A model is a formula that a computer learns from examples. A linear model adds up the features, each multiplied by a number (a coefficient) that it learns from the data. A non-linear model can also learn curved relationships.

Evaluation Criteria

To measure how good a model is, we use the root mean squared error (RMSE) between the log of the predicted price and the log of the actual SalePrice. RMSE is the typical size of a prediction error, so a lower RMSE is better. We use the log of the prices so that an error of 10% counts the same for an expensive house and for a cheap house.

Steps for Building Models

Each model has settings that it cannot learn from the data. We must choose them before training. These settings are called hyperparameters. To choose the best hyperparameters, we use K-fold cross validation, as described in the steps below:

  • Remove features that repeat the information of other features, and change ordinal features into scores.
  • Split the training data into K parts (folds). Each time, the model learns from all the folds except one (the training part), and we check its predictions on the remaining fold (the validation part). We split the data in a way that keeps a similar mix of prices in each fold (stratified sampling).
  • Choose the linear and non-linear models to use.
  • For each model, make a set (a grid) of hyperparameter combinations that covers the possible values evenly (a space-filling grid).
  • For each combination, train the model on the training part and make predictions on the validation part. Repeat this for all the folds.
  • Calculate the RMSE, and choose the combination with the lowest RMSE.
  • Train each model again, with its best combination, on the complete training set.
  • Calculate the RMSE of each final model on the testing set, which has properties that the models have not seen.
  • Choose the model with the lowest RMSE.

Removing Collinear Predictors

Many features in this dataset describe the same thing in different ways. Also, some of the features that we created in the previous post repeat others. A model cannot use categories directly, so each category becomes a separate feature with the values 0 and 1 (a dummy variable). After this change, some features are exact combinations of other features (we call them collinear). A linear model cannot separate the effects of collinear features. So its coefficients become unreliable, or it cannot calculate them at all, and lm (the basic linear model in R) gives a warning about a “rank-deficient fit”. Models that use decision trees are not affected by repeated information. But if we remove it, the linear models work correctly and all the models are simpler.

The association matrix in the previous post showed which features repeat each other. We drop these features, because other features already give their information:

  • HasGarage, HasFireplace and HasMasVnr are the same as, or almost the same as, the None category of GarageType, FireplaceQu and MasVnrType.
  • MSSubClass combines the type and the style of a building. BldgType and HouseStyle already give this information. Its duplex category is identical to the duplex category of BldgType.
  • TotalBath is exactly FullBath + 0.5 * HalfBath + BsmtBath. We drop HalfBath, not TotalBath. So we keep the total, which is one of the most important features for the decision tree models. And we lose no information, because we can calculate HalfBath from the other three features.

Encoding Ordinal Features

The categories of features such as OverallQual or KitchenQual have a natural order. These are ordinal features. By default, step_dummy() changes an ordinal feature into several features called polynomial contrasts. It makes one new feature for each category except one, and these features describe straight, curved and more complex trends across the grades. But some grades are very rare. For example, only one property has an OverallCond of 1. So a rare grade can be missing from a fold. Then some of these new features become collinear in that fold.

Instead, we change each ordinal feature into one whole number (a score) that follows the order of its categories: 1, 2, 3 and so on. This assumes that the steps between the grades are equal. First, we drop the categories that no property has, such as a Poor exterior quality, so that the scores have no gaps. Here are the results of a linear model with each method, on the same folds:

dfEncodingComparison %>% 
  mutate(lm_cv_rmse = round(lm_cv_rmse, 4)) %>% 
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Encoding of ordinal features", "Predictors", "Folds with a rank-deficient fit", "lm cross validated RMSE"))
Encoding of ordinal features Predictors Folds with a rank-deficient fit lm cross validated RMSE
polynomial contrasts 214 4 0.1470
ordinal scores 151 0 0.1336 
encoding_value <- function(encodingName, column) dfEncodingComparison[[column]][dfEncodingComparison$encoding == encodingName]
  • With polynomial contrasts, lm cannot calculate all the coefficients in 4 of the 5 folds. With scores, this problem happens in 0 folds.
  • With scores, the number of features goes down from 214 to 151, and the cross validated RMSE of lm goes down from 0.147 to 0.134. The simpler method works better on new data, because the model does not have to learn a separate effect for each rare grade.

Finally, step_lincomb() checks whether any features are still exact combinations of other features. This could happen because properties without a basement or a garage have the None category in every basement or garage feature. With scores, it finds no such features.

After these steps, there are 151 features, and a linear model can calculate a coefficient for each of them:

model_lm_check <- lm(target ~ ., data = dfTrain_Proc %>% select(-Id))
print(glue::glue("{sum(is.na(coef(model_lm_check)))} of {length(coef(model_lm_check))} coefficients could not be estimated"))
0 of 152 coefficients could not be estimated

Partitioning Training Data

We split the training data into 5 folds. In each fold, the model learns from 80% of the data, and we compare its predictions with the actual prices on the other 20%.

Let’s look at the spread (distribution) of the target, which is the value that we want to predict, in all the folds:

cv_folds %>% 
  mutate(target = map(splits, function(Z) bind_rows(training(Z) %>% select(target) %>% mutate(type = "training"), 
                                                    testing(Z) %>% select(target) %>% mutate(type = "validation")))) %>% 
  select(-splits) %>% 
  unnest(cols = c(target)) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = target)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, color = "white", fill = "#F37735") +
  labs(x = "log(SalePrice)") +
  facet_grid(type ~ id)

Because we use stratified sampling, the prices have similar distributions in the training part and in the validation part of each fold.

Linear Models

Ordinary Least Squares Regression

First, we use cross validation to test a simple linear model on the training data. This model, called ordinary least squares, finds the straight-line formula with the smallest squared errors. Its result is our starting point (benchmark). If more complex models are not much better than this result, they are not worth the extra effort.

model_spec_lm
Linear Regression Model Specification (regression)

Computational engine: lm 
cv_results_lm
# A tibble: 1 × 1
  mean_rmse
      <dbl>
1     0.134
rmse_val <- cv_results_lm %>% pull(mean_rmse)

What’s notable?

  • A linear model with all the features gives an RMSE of 0.1336.
  • This is the simplest and fastest model, and it has no hyperparameters to choose.

Regularized Linear Model

Next, we use glmnet, a linear model with regularization. Regularization adds a penalty for large coefficients. This makes the model keep only the effects that the data clearly supports. glmnet combines two types of regularization: LASSO (L1), which can reduce the coefficient of a feature to exactly 0, and Ridge (L2), which makes all the coefficients smaller. We search for the values of these hyperparameters that give the lowest RMSE:

  • penalty: the total amount of regularization in the model.
  • mixture: the share of LASSO (L1) regularization in the model.
model_spec_glmnet
Linear Regression Model Specification (regression)

Main Arguments:
  penalty = tune()
  mixture = tune()

Computational engine: glmnet

Here are the 10 best RMSE values and their hyperparameter combinations:

cv_results_glmnet %>% head(10)
# A tibble: 10 × 3
    penalty mixture mean_rmse
      <dbl>   <dbl>     <dbl>
 1 1.46e- 2  0.297      0.129
 2 1.22e- 3  0.490      0.130
 3 1.09e- 2  0.0439     0.131
 4 3.47e- 4  0.992      0.131
 5 1.22e- 2  0.657      0.131
 6 8.18e- 4  0.0856     0.132
 7 7.37e- 7  0.0221     0.132
 8 1.15e- 4  0.798      0.132
 9 3.37e-10  0.0573     0.133
10 1.57e- 5  0.0760     0.133

What’s notable?

  • After we choose the hyperparameters with cross validation, the best glmnet model has an RMSE of 0.129, with penalty = 0.0146 and mixture = 0.2974.
  • This is better than the ordinary least squares model, which had an RMSE of 0.1336. The regularization makes the coefficients of the less useful features smaller. This helps when there are so many features.
  • Cross validation of glmnet is fast. It takes about 11 seconds.
  • But outliers can strongly affect its results.

Here is a plot of the glmnet hyperparameter grid, with the best combination:

eda_plot_scatter(param_grid_glmnet, "mixture", "penalty", alpha = 1, add_lm = F, yLog = T, yLabelsScale = scales::scientific) +
  geom_point(data = param_best_glmnet, aes(x = mixture, y = penalty), color = "red") +
  ggrepel::geom_label_repel(data = param_best_glmnet %>% map_df(round, digits = 4), 
                            aes(x = mixture, y = penalty, label = glue::glue("penalty: {penalty}, mixture:{mixture}")),
                            family = "Roboto Condensed")

Non-linear Models

Next, we train two types of models that use decision trees. A decision tree predicts a value by asking a series of yes/no questions about the features, such as “Is TotalSF more than 2000?”. These models are not very sensitive to outliers and skewed data.

ranger (Random Forest)

A random forest builds many decision trees, each from a random sample of the data, and takes the average of their predictions. We use ranger, a version of random forests that gives the same results as the randomForest package but runs about 3 times faster. Each forest has 500 trees. (On a dataset of this size, more trees do not improve the error.) We search for the best values of these hyperparameters:

  • mtry: the number of features that the tree chooses from at random at each question (split).
  • min_n: the minimum number of properties that a group (node) must have before the tree can split it again.
model_spec_rf
Random Forest Model Specification (regression)

Main Arguments:
  mtry = tune()
  trees = 500
  min_n = tune()

Engine-Specific Arguments:
  num.threads = 1

Computational engine: ranger

Here are the 10 best RMSE values and their hyperparameter combinations:

cv_results_rf %>% head(10)
# A tibble: 10 × 3
   min_n  mtry mean_rmse
   <int> <int>     <dbl>

10    33    46     0.138

What’s notable?

  • After cross validation, the best RMSE is 0.132, with mtry = 51 and min_n = 2.
  • This is not better than glmnet. Also, cross validation of ranger takes much longer: about 164 seconds, against 11 seconds for glmnet.

Here is a plot of the ranger hyperparameter grid, with the best combination:

eda_plot_scatter(param_grid_rf, "min_n", "mtry", alpha = 1, add_lm = F) +
  geom_point(data = param_best_rf, aes(x = min_n, y = mtry), color = "red") +

xgboost

xgboost (gradient boosting) builds decision trees one after the other. Each new tree corrects some of the errors of the trees before it. Each model has 1000 trees, and we search for the best values of these hyperparameters:

  • min_n: the minimum number of properties that a group (node) must have before the tree can split it again.
  • tree_depth: the maximum number of questions (splits) from the top of a tree to its bottom.
  • learn_rate: how much each new tree can change the predictions. A smaller value makes the model learn more slowly and carefully.
model_spec_xgboost
Boosted Tree Model Specification (regression)

Main Arguments:
  trees = 1000
  min_n = tune()
  tree_depth = tune()
  learn_rate = tune()

Engine-Specific Arguments:
  objective = reg:squarederror
  nthread = 1

Computational engine: xgboost

Here are the 10 best RMSE values and their hyperparameter combinations:

cv_results_xgboost %>% head(10)
# A tibble: 10 × 4
   min_n tree_depth learn_rate mean_rmse
   <int>      <int>      <dbl>     <dbl>
 1    33          2    0.0289      0.125
 2     3          2    0.0171      0.127
 3    23          4    0.0254      0.128
 4    24          1    0.190       0.129
 5    11          5    0.0549      0.129
 6    32          9    0.00605     0.130
 7    19         11    0.00482     0.130
 8    16         14    0.0121      0.131
 9    38          9    0.0270      0.131
10    23          9    0.0405      0.131

What’s notable?

  • After cross validation, the best RMSE is 0.125, with min_n = 33, tree_depth = 2 and learn_rate = 0.0289.
  • This is the best cross validated RMSE of all the models. It is a little better than glmnet (0.129) and ranger (0.132).
  • Cross validation of xgboost takes longer than glmnet, but it is faster than ranger (about 137 seconds).

Finalizing Models

For each model, we now know the hyperparameters with the lowest RMSE. We use them to train each model again on the complete training set. Then we use the trained models to predict log(SalePrice) for the training set, and we compare the predictions with the actual values.

# Get predicted estimates
get_predicted <- function(model_final, dfNew) {

  # Predict on testing set
  vEstimates <- model_final %>%
    predict(new_data = dfNew) %>%
    pull(.pred)
  
  return(vEstimates)
}

dfResults_train <- dfTrain %>% 
  mutate(actual = log(SalePrice)) %>% 
  select(Id, actual) %>% 
  mutate(glmnet = get_predicted(model_final = model_final_glmnet, dfTrain_Proc),
         ranger = get_predicted(model_final = model_final_rf, dfTrain_Proc),
         xgboost = get_predicted(model_final = model_final_xgboost, dfTrain_Proc))
dfPlot <- dfResults_train %>% 
  gather(model, predicted, -actual, -Id) %>% 
  mutate(model = ordered(model, levels = c("glmnet","ranger","xgboost")))

dfPlot %>%
  rename(`log(SalePrice)` = actual) %>%
  eda_plot_actual_vs_predicted("log(SalePrice)", "predicted", feature_model = "model", feature_id = "Id", nLabel = 3) +
  labs(title = "Actual v/s predicted log(SalePrice) on training set")

# properties among the 3 largest errors of more than one model
dfWorst_train <- dfPlot %>%
  group_by(model) %>%
  slice_max(abs(predicted - actual), n = 3) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  count(Id, name = "n_models") %>%
  filter(n_models > 1) %>%
  arrange(desc(n_models))

# sentence about the properties that are among the largest errors of the most models
worst_train_sentence <- if (nrow(dfWorst_train) == 0) {
  "No property is among them for more than one model."
} else {
  vIds <- dfWorst_train$Id[dfWorst_train$n_models == max(dfWorst_train$n_models)]
  glue::glue("{if (length(vIds) == 1) 'The property with Id' else 'The properties with Ids'} {paste0('__', vIds, '__', collapse = ' and ')} {if (length(vIds) == 1) 'is' else 'are each'} among them for {max(dfWorst_train$n_models)} of the 3 models, so we should check {if (length(vIds) == 1) 'its' else 'their'} data for errors.")
}

What’s notable?

  • ranger and xgboost fit the training data closely: their predictions are near the 45-degree line, where the predicted value is equal to the actual value. ranger fits the training data most closely, with a training RMSE of 0.050, against 0.096 for xgboost.
  • The glmnet model has two outliers, Ids 524 and 1299. Their predicted prices are much higher than their actual prices. Also, for the cheaper properties, the predicted values are very spread out.
  • The plots label the three largest errors of each model. The properties with Ids 31 and 1299 are each among them for 2 of the 3 models, so we should check their data for errors.
  • But a good fit on the training data does not prove that a model is good. We can only measure its true performance on data that it has not seen: the testing set.

Performance on Test Data

dfResults_test <- dfTest %>% 
  mutate(actual = log(SalePrice)) %>% 
  select(Id, actual) %>% 
  mutate(glmnet = get_predicted(model_final = model_final_glmnet, dfTest_Proc),
         ranger = get_predicted(model_final = model_final_rf, dfTest_Proc),
         xgboost = get_predicted(model_final = model_final_xgboost, dfTest_Proc))
dfPlot <- dfResults_test %>% 
  gather(model, predicted, -actual, -Id) %>% 
  mutate(model = ordered(model, levels = c("glmnet","ranger","xgboost")))

dfPlot %>%
  rename(`log(SalePrice)` = actual) %>%
  eda_plot_actual_vs_predicted("log(SalePrice)", "predicted", feature_model = "model", feature_id = "Id", nLabel = 3) +
  labs(title = "Actual v/s predicted log(SalePrice) on testing set")

dfRMSE <- map(list("glmnet","ranger","xgboost"), ~ rmse(dfResults_test, actual, !!sym(.x)) %>% mutate(model = .x)) %>%
  bind_rows() %>%
  mutate(cv_rmse = c(cv_results_glmnet$mean_rmse[1], cv_results_rf$mean_rmse[1], cv_results_xgboost$mean_rmse[1])) %>%
  select(-.estimator, -.metric) %>%
  rename(test_rmse = .estimate) %>%
  select(model, everything())

dfRMSE
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  model   test_rmse cv_rmse
  <chr>       <dbl>   <dbl>
1 glmnet      0.130   0.129
2 ranger      0.138   0.132
3 xgboost     0.132   0.125

What’s notable?

  • For all the models, the RMSE on the testing set is similar to the cross validated RMSE. This shows that cross validation correctly estimated how well the models work on new data, and that the hyperparameters are good.
  • The properties with Ids 1537 and 2217 are outliers: no model predicts a price close to their actual prices.
  • glmnet has the lowest RMSE on the testing set, 0.130. xgboost is close, with 0.132.
  • But outliers affect glmnet, as we saw with Ids 524 and 1299 in the training set. xgboost had the best cross validated RMSE, and the difference on the testing set is small. Also, xgboost is less affected by outliers, and it can learn curved relationships. So we choose xgboost as our final model, because it works well on new data.
model_final <- model_final_xgboost

Feature Importance

It is harder to understand how xgboost makes its predictions than how a linear model makes them. But a variable importance plot can show which features are the most important for the model.

Here are the 10 most important features of our final xgboost model:

library(vip)

p1 <- vip(extract_fit_parsnip(model_final), aesthetics = list(fill = "#00AED8")) +
  labs(title = "xgboost model Feature Importance in Training") +
  theme_quant()

vFeaturesImp <- vip::vi(extract_fit_parsnip(model_final)) %>% top_n(10, Importance) %>% pull(Variable)

p2 <- eda_plot_correlation_matrix(dfTrain %>% select(SalePrice, one_of(vFeaturesImp)), 
                            outlineVar = "SalePrice", plotTitle = "Correlations with SalePrice")

cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = list(p1, p2), nrow = 1)

  • The plot on the right shows the correlations of the numerical features. All of them have a correlation of at least 0.5, or at most -0.5, with SalePrice.
  • All of the 10 most important features make sense. To judge the price of a property, a buyer would look at the total area, the overall quality, the neighborhood, the number of bathrooms, the kitchen quality, the age of the property, the size and finish of the garage, central air conditioning, the overall condition, and so on.
  • So our final model works well on new data, and it chooses very reasonable features.

New Property Premium

Of the 10 most important features in our final model, most do not change during the life of a property, such as the area, the neighborhood and the number of bathrooms. The quality and the condition of a property can change, but people judge them in different ways. The only feature that clearly changes over time is PropertyAge.

So, how does the predicted SalePrice change with the age of a property? We compare the same property when it is new, when it is more than 30 years old, and at all the ages in between.

We choose two properties at random, change their PropertyAge, and look at the effect on the predicted SalePrice.

getSampleProperty <- function(randomSeed) {
  
  set.seed(randomSeed)
  dfSample <- dfTest %>% 
    filter(PropertyAge >= 30) %>% 
    sample_n(1)
  
  dfSample <- tibble(PropertyAge = 1:dfSample$PropertyAge[1]) %>% expand_grid(dfSample %>% select(-PropertyAge))
}

dfSample <- getSampleProperty(1000) %>% bind_rows(getSampleProperty(2000))

# preprocess the sample data with the recipe prepared on the training set and generate predicted values from the final model
bake(preprocessing_recipe, new_data = dfSample) %>% 
  get_predicted(model_final, .) %>% 
  as_tibble() %>% 
  bind_cols(dfSample) %>% 
  mutate(predicted = exp(value)) %>% 
  group_by(Id) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = PropertyAge, y = predicted)) +
  geom_point(color = "#00AED8") +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~Id, scales = "free") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(y = "Predicted Sale Price",
       title = "New Property Premium")

A new property sells for a little more than an older property of the same type, quality and condition. This premium is small in a place like Ames, Iowa. We expect it to be much higher in a large city.

item.title: Diamonds - Part 3 - A polished gem - Building Non-linear Models
item.description:
Other posts in this series:

  • Diamonds - Part 1 - In the rough - An Exploratory Data Analysis
  • Diamonds - Part 2 - A cut above - Building Linear Models

In the previous posts, we found out which attributes of a diamond are important for its price. An exploratory data analysis showed that carat, clarity and color are the most important features to predict price. Then we built linear models to predict the prices, and we chose the best model by its metrics.

In this post, we use non-linear models to predict the prices of diamonds, and we compare them with the linear models. A non-linear model can learn curved relationships and interactions between features by itself.

Training Non-linear Models

We use three types of non-linear models:

  • randomForest builds many decision trees and takes the average of their predictions. A decision tree predicts a value by asking a series of yes/no questions about the features, such as “Is carat more than 1?”.
  • xgboost (gradient boosting) builds many small decision trees one after the other. Each new tree corrects some of the errors of the trees before it.
  • keras builds a neural network. A neural network passes the features through layers of simple calculations, and it learns the strength of each connection from the data.

We follow some of the same steps as for the linear models, and we change some features:

  • Split the dataset into a training set with 75% of the diamonds and a testing set with 25%.
  • Keep the same mix of clarity grades in both sets (stratified sampling).
  • clarity, color and cut have ordered categories, from the lowest grade to the highest grade. randomForest can use these categories directly. But xgboost and keras need all the features as numbers. There are two methods to change categories into numbers:
    1. One-hot encoding: each category of clarity, color and cut becomes a new feature with the values 0 and 1. A disadvantage of this method is that the order of the grades is lost. But the training set is large, so the non-linear models can learn the order by themselves.
    2. Integer scores: the grades become the numbers 1, 2, 3 and so on, from the lowest grade to the highest. But this method assumes that the steps between all the grades are equal, which may not be correct here.
  • Center and scale all the values in the training set, so that all the features have similar ranges. Then put the features in a matrix (a table of numbers).
  • Train a non-linear model on the training set.
  • Make predictions on the testing set and calculate the metrics.
  • Put all the steps above in a function that takes the model formula and a random seed. The seed controls the random split into the training set and the testing set.
  • Run each model several times with different seeds, and calculate its average metrics. These averages show how well the model works on new data.

Here are the average metrics for all the models that we trained with keras, randomForest and xgboost:

load("fit_models_keras.Rda")

dfModels_keras <- dfModels %>% mutate(type = "keras")
best_model_results_keras <- best_model_results
dfResults_keras <- best_model_results_keras$dfResults %>% mutate(type = "keras")

load("fit_models_rf.Rda")

dfModels_rf <- dfModels %>% mutate(type = "randomForest")
best_model_results_rf <- best_model_results
dfResults_rf <- best_model_results_rf$dfResults %>% mutate(type = "randomForest")

load("fit_models_xgb.Rda")

dfModels_xgb <- dfModels %>% mutate(type = "xgboost")
best_model_results_xgb <- best_model_results
dfResults_xgb <- best_model_results_xgb$dfResults %>% mutate(type = "xgboost")

# combine the actual v/s predicted results from the best model using the 3 methods
dfResults <- map_df(list(dfResults_keras, dfResults_rf, dfResults_xgb), bind_rows) %>% 
  select(type, everything()) %>% 
  mutate_if(is.numeric, ~ round(.x, digits = 2)) %>% 
  group_by(type)

# combine the average metrics from all the models using the 3 methods
dfModels <- map_df(list(dfModels_keras, dfModels_rf, dfModels_xgb), bind_rows) %>% 
  select(type, everything()) %>% 
  mutate_if(is.numeric, ~ round(.x, digits = 2)) %>% 
  gather(avg_metric, value, rmse, rsq, mae)

# create an HTML table
dfModels %>% tidyHtmlTable(header = "type", cgroup1 = "avg_metric", cell_value = "value", rnames = "model", align = "|rrr|rrr|rrr")
keras randomForest xgboost
price ~ . c(“989.71”, “0.93”, “360.55”) c(“529.28”, “0.98”, “262.35”) c(“540.76”, “0.98”, “280.49”)
price ~ carat c(“1499.2”, “0.86”, “860.29”) c(“1427.25”, “0.87”, “816.1”) c(“1427.35”, “0.87”, “815.76”)
price ~ carat + clarity c(“1040.69”, “0.93”, “590.32”) c(“1006.61”, “0.94”, “548.67”) c(“992.46”, “0.94”, “544.48”)
price ~ carat + clarity + color c(“645.4”, “0.97”, “358.85”) c(“571.73”, “0.98”, “305.17”) c(“575.3”, “0.98”, “306.86”)
price ~ carat + clarity + color + cut c(“626.78”, “0.98”, “347.99”) c(“545.02”, “0.98”, “285.96”) c(“541.63”, “0.98”, “282.38”)

The R-squared values (rsq) show that all the models learn the complex relationship between price and carat very well. For the linear models, we had to change both price and carat to a log scale. The neural network and the decision tree models learn this relationship by themselves. The root mean squared error (RMSE) is in dollars, so it is easy to understand. The average price of a diamond is about $4000, and the prices vary by about $4000 (the standard deviation). So the RMSE values of the models are very low. With carat, clarity and color, the RMSE is between $572 and $645. The best linear model with the same features has an RMSE of about $816.

The exploratory data analysis helps here, because the models with only carat, clarity and color give excellent results. If we add cut, the RMSE goes down only a little.

Even the base models with all the features (price ~ .) explain the variation in the prices very well, although some of their features repeat the same information. Decision trees and neural networks are not affected by such repeated information (multicollinearity) as much as linear models are. To find the most important features of these models, we can explain their predictions one at a time.

Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations

LIME is a method to explain the predictions of a “black box” model, which is a model whose calculations are too complex for a person to follow. LIME explains one prediction at a time. It assumes that, close to a single diamond, the complex model behaves like a simple linear model. So LIME fits a simple model around that one diamond. The simple model then explains how the complex model makes its prediction for that diamond.

LIME uses these steps:

  • Take one diamond, and make many copies of it with small random changes to its features.
  • Measure how similar each copy is to the original diamond.
  • Use the complex model to predict the price of each copy.
  • Choose a small number (m) of features that best explain the predicted prices.
  • Fit a simple model to the copies, with the m features. Give more weight to the copies that are more similar to the original diamond.
  • Use the weights of the simple model to explain the prediction for the original diamond.

Here, we choose the 5 features that best explain the predictions for 6 random diamonds from the testing set.

# Plot Feature Importance by sample
plot_features(explanation_keras, ncol = 3) + 
  labs(title = "LIME Feature Importance from a keras model",
       subtitle = glue::glue("{numSamples} random samples from testing set")) +
  theme_quant() +
  theme(plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

plot_features(explanation_xgb, ncol = 3) + 
  labs(title = "LIME Feature Importance from an xgboost model",
       subtitle = glue::glue("{numSamples} random samples from testing set")) +
  theme_quant() +
  theme(plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

For these 6 random diamonds, the most important features for the predictions are carat, clarity, color, x and y.

# Plot Feature Importance Heatmap
plot_explanations(explanation_keras) +
  labs(title = "LIME Feature Importance Heatmap from a keras model",
       subtitle = glue::glue("{numSamples} random samples from testing set")) +
  theme_quant() +
  theme(plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

plot_explanations(explanation_xgb) +
  labs(title = "LIME Feature Importance Heatmap from an xgboost model",
       subtitle = glue::glue("{numSamples} random samples from testing set")) +
  theme_quant() +
  theme(plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

We know that x and y have a very strong correlation with carat, so they repeat the same information. That is why it is good practice to remove such repeated features before we train a model. For keras, the model with carat, clarity and color has the best metrics. For the decision tree models, the model with all the features is a little more accurate, but it needs many more features.

Actual v/s Predicted

Finally, here are the scatter plots of the actual prices against the predicted prices, for the best model of each type on the testing set:

p1 <- dfResults %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  rename(price = actual) %>%
  eda_plot_actual_vs_predicted("price", "estimate", feature_model = "type", nLabel = 0,
                               labelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(title = paste(formulaString_best, "(linear scale)")) +
  theme(panel.spacing.x = unit(2, "lines"), plot.margin = margin(5, 25, 5, 5))

p2 <- dfResults %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  rename(price = actual) %>%
  eda_plot_actual_vs_predicted("price", "estimate", feature_model = "type", nLabel = 0, xLog = T, yLog = T,
                               labelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(title = paste(formulaString_best, "(log scale)")) +
  theme(panel.spacing.x = unit(2, "lines"), plot.margin = margin(5, 25, 5, 5))

cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = list(p1, p2), ncol = 1)

The scatter plots use both normal (linear) axes and log axes. The R-squared and RMSE values of the 3 methods are similar. But for expensive diamonds, the predictions of keras are more spread out than the predictions of the two decision tree methods. For cheap diamonds, the decision tree methods seem to predict the prices better, with less spread.

As with the linear models, the spread of the predicted prices increases with price. The decision tree methods keep their predictions close to the range of prices in the data. Their highest predictions are $18,340 (randomForest) and $19,118 (xgboost). The most expensive diamond in the testing set costs $18,823. A randomForest prediction is an average of prices from the training data, so it cannot be higher than those prices. xgboost adds up many small corrections, so its predictions can be only a little higher. A neural network, like a linear model, can predict prices far above the prices in the data (extrapolation). The highest price that keras predicts is $26,591. So the non-linear methods learn the relationships between price and the other features very well, and the decision tree methods also keep their predictions within a reasonable range.

Summary

  • All 3 non-linear methods learn the complex relationship between price, carat and the other features by themselves. They do not need feature engineering.
  • The exploratory data analysis helps us remove repeated features before we train the models. This makes the training faster. For keras, it also gives much better metrics.
  • keras neural networks train the fastest, because they can use a GPU (a graphics processor that does many calculations at the same time).
  • Of the two decision tree methods, xgboost trains much faster than randomForest.
  • randomForest and xgboost can use several CPU cores at the same time. On a local computer, the amount of memory (RAM) is the only limit.

item.title: Diamonds - Part 2 - A cut above - Building Linear Models
item.description:
In a previous post in this series, we explored the diamonds dataset. We found that price has a strong correlation with carat, x, y and z, and that log(price) has an almost straight-line relationship with log(carat). For diamonds of similar weight, clarity and color also seemed to help predict the price.

In this post, we build linear models and find out how well they predict the price of diamonds. A linear model predicts a value by adding up the features, each multiplied by a number (a coefficient) that the model learns from the data.

First, let’s build a simple base model that uses all the features, without any changes to them. Its results give us a starting point to compare with:

The model summary shows that this model is overfitted. An overfitted model learns the noise in the data, not only the true patterns, so it does not work well on new data. For example, we know that depth and table have no effect on price, but the model says that they are very important.

The table above also shows the root mean squared error (RMSE) and other metrics. RMSE is the typical size of a prediction error, in the same units as the price. A lower RMSE means better predictions.

Let’s plot the actual prices against the predicted prices, to see how well this base model works.

augment(model_lm, diamonds) %>%
  eda_plot_actual_vs_predicted("price", ".fitted", nLabel = 0, labelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(title = "Actual v/s predicted price from a base linear model")

If the predictions are good, the points are close to the dashed line at 45 degrees, where the predicted price is equal to the actual price. This base model predicts the prices badly. Worst of all, it predicts negative prices for cheap diamonds. To prevent such impossible results, we must use log(price) instead of price.

Feature Engineering

Feature engineering means that we create new features from the existing features, to make the patterns easier for a model to learn.

We know that the price of a diamond has a strong correlation with its size. If all other things are equal, a larger diamond has a higher price.

As a first estimate, we can treat a diamond as a box with the dimensions x, y and z. Then its volume is x * y * z. These 3 dimensions have a strong correlation with each other. So we can calculate one average dimension as the cube root of volume. This average dimension keeps a straight-line relationship with log(price).

We can also calculate an average dimension with high school chemistry. Mass, volume and density are related by this equation:

$ density = mass/volume $

1 carat is 0.2 grams. If we divide the mass by the density of diamond (3.51 grams per cubic centimeter), we get the volume. The cube root of the volume gives an average dimension.

dfInput <- diamonds %>%
  mutate(row = row_number(),
         volume = x*y*z,
         `average dimension` = volume ^ (1/3),
         volume2 = carat * 0.2/3.51,
         `average dimension2` = (volume2 ^ (1/3)) * 10)   # Multiply by 10 to convert from cm to mm

eda_plot_scatter(dfInput, c("average dimension", "average dimension2"), "price", yLabelsScale = scales::dollar,
                 nLabel = 3, feature_id = "row", labelBy = "leverage") +
  labs(title = "Scatterplot of price v/s average dimension")

# the point with the most leverage on the linear fit of price on the dimension-based feature
dfLeverage <- dfInput %>%
  mutate(leverage = hatvalues(lm(price ~ `average dimension`, data = dfInput))) %>%
  slice_max(leverage, n = 1)

The two methods give similar results, but the density method gives a narrower range. Which method is more reliable? In each panel, the labels show the row numbers of the diamonds with the most leverage. Leverage tells how much a point can pull the straight line towards itself. Points that are far from the others along the x axis have the most leverage. With the dimensions, the most extreme point is the diamond in row 24068. It is a 2 carat diamond with a recorded width y of 58.9 mm. This value is clearly a recording error. The other labelled points are diamonds with an average dimension of 0. With the density method, the labelled points are simply the largest diamonds in the dataset. Also, 20 values of z are 0. In 7 of these diamonds, x and y are also 0. So these dimensions were not recorded correctly.

For all of these diamonds, the carat values are correct. So carat is probably more accurate than the dimensions, and we prefer the density method to create this feature.

Also, the density is a constant. So we do not need to divide by it to calculate the volume. Instead, we can take the cube root of carat itself. Then we expect a straight-line relationship between \(log(price)\) and \(carat^{1/3}\). A straight-line relationship is what a linear model needs, because the model adds up its features in a straight-line way.

The geometry suggests a cube root. But does the cube root give the best straight line? Let’s compare it with other transforms. Each panel shows the R-squared of a straight line through the points of log(price):

p_transforms <- eda_plot_transforms(diamonds, "carat", "price")
p_transforms

# R-squared of each transform, in the order of the panels
vR2_carat <- p_transforms$data %>%
  distinct(transform, r_squared) %>%
  pull(r_squared) %>%
  set_names(c("identity", "log", "sqrt", "cuberoot"))

The cube root (R-squared 0.924) is much better than carat without a transform (0.847). But log(carat) is even better (0.933). A straight-line relationship between \(log(price)\) and \(log(carat)\) is easy to understand: the coefficient of \(log(carat)\) is the percentage change in price when carat increases by 1%. We will try both transforms in our models.

Training Linear Models

These are the steps to build the linear models and measure how well they work:

  • Split the dataset into two sets: a training set with 75% of the diamonds and a testing set with 25%. The model learns from the training set. Then we check its predictions on the testing set, which has diamonds that the model has not seen.
  • clarity is one of the most important features. So we split the data in a way that keeps the same mix of clarity grades in both sets. This is called stratified sampling.
  • Train (fit) a linear model on the training set.
  • Make predictions on the testing set and calculate the metrics.
  • Put all the steps above in a function that takes the model formula and a random seed. The seed controls which diamonds go into each set. With different seeds, we get different random splits, so one lucky or unlucky split does not decide the results.
  • Run each model several times with different seeds, and calculate its average metrics. These averages show how well the model works on new data.

Here is one split into a training set and a testing set, stratified by clarity. Both sets have a similar mix of clarity grades.

set.seed(1333)
train_split <- diamonds %>% 
  select(price, everything()) %>% 
  initial_split(prop = 0.75, strata = "clarity")

dfTrain <- training(train_split)
dfTest <- testing(train_split)

We ran each model 5 times with different seeds. Here are the average metrics. R-squared (rsq) tells how much of the variation in price the model explains, and the mean absolute error (mae) is the average size of a prediction error:

fit_linear_model <- function(randomSeed, model_formula, get_model = FALSE) {

  set.seed(randomSeed)
  train_split <- diamonds %>% 
    select(price, everything()) %>% 
    initial_split(prop = 0.75, strata = "clarity")
  
  dfTrain <- training(train_split)
  dfTest <- testing(train_split)

  # fit a linear model
  model_lm <- lm(model_formula, data = dfTrain)
  
  # predict on testing set to determine rmse  
  predict_lm <- predict(model_lm, dfTest)

  # predict on testing set with outliers
  dfResults <- dfTest %>% 
    mutate(actual = price) %>% 
    mutate(estimate = predict_lm %>% exp()) %>% 
    select(actual, estimate)
  
  if(get_model) {
    return(list(model_lm, dfResults))
  } else {
    return(dfResults)
  }
}
set.seed(1000)
vRandomSeeds <- sample(9999, 5)
dfModels <- expand_grid(seed = vRandomSeeds, 
                        model = c("log(price) ~ .",
                                  "log(price) ~ I(carat^(1/3))",
                                  "log(price) ~ I(carat^(1/3)) + clarity",
                                  "log(price) ~ I(carat^(1/3)) + clarity + color",
                                  "log(price) ~ I(carat^(1/3)) + clarity + color + cut",
                                  "log(price) ~ log(carat)",
                                  "log(price) ~ log(carat) + clarity",
                                  "log(price) ~ log(carat) + clarity + color",
                                  "log(price) ~ log(carat) + clarity + color + cut")) %>%
  mutate(results = map2(seed, model, ~ fit_linear_model(.x, as.formula(.y)))) %>% 
  mutate(metrics = map(results, ~ metrics(.x, truth = actual, estimate = estimate))) %>%
  select(-results) %>% 
  unnest(cols = metrics) %>% 
  select(-.estimator) %>% 
  spread(.metric, .estimate) %>% 
  group_by(model) %>% 
  summarise_at(vars(rmse, rsq, mae), mean)

item.title: Building blocks of systematic investment strategies
item.description:
It is important to understand the building blocks of systematic investing strategies before learning how to build them. Here is a schematic from the book, Inside the Black Box - The Simple Truth about Quantitative Trading by Rishi Narang, that provides a good way to visualize these building blocks and how they fit together in a system.

The Black Box Revealed

The author had aptly titled it - The Black Box Revealed, since that is how most people perceive it to be from the outside. From this schematic, it is easier to understand and visualize how a system is built with a systematic approach.

Here are the components of the system:

  • Data - Encapsulates the processes of raw data collection, cleaning and preparation in tidy form to be used by the models.
  • Alpha Model - Describes the core strategy, product universe (stocks, ETFs, futures) and the rules to be implemented.
  • Risk Model - Describes position sizes or how capital/risk is allocated. This is just as much important as the alpha model itself.
  • Transaction Cost Model - Describes the transaction costs by product. These may be theoretical numbers while backtesting the strategy using historical data and later adjusted based on live execution data.
  • Portfolio Construction Model - Describes how a portfolio is constructed after putting together positions by product across one or more rules of the core strategy.
  • Execution Model - Encapsulates a live trading system. Describes the tactical implementation of the core strategy.
  • Research - Sound research forms the underpinning of all models and is driven by quantitative and statistical analysis.

The interactions shown are typical, although there could be more depending upon the implementation. More than one model could also be combined together, depending upon how the strategy is formulated. Nonetheless, for most practitioners looking to build a complete system from scratch, this is a pretty good blueprint.
